children: OTTAWA--Canada's budget deficit for the first quarter of the current fiscal year is sharply narrower from the prior year, buoyed by strong gains in personal and sales-tax receipts.
The data may reflect the income gains Canada is netting as a net exporter of crude oil, with energy prices higher as a result of the U.S.-Iran conflict.

Canada's Department of Finance said the government recorded a budget surplus of 989 million Canadian dollars (US$713.8 million) in June, or smaller than the C$3.63 billion surplus from the same year-ago month. For the first three months of the 2026-27 fiscal year, Canada is running a relatively small deficit of C$370 million, versus a C$6.28 billion deficit for the comparable year-ago period.
In April, Canada said it was projecting a C$66.9 billion deficit for the 2026-27 fiscal year, which ends on March 31 of next year.

The data, courtesy of the finance ministry's Fiscal Monitor publication, emerged on the same day as Statistics Canada said Canada's economy grew by a robust 3.3% annualized pace in the April-to-June period. The data indicated notable gains in household after-tax income and corporate earnings, which bodes well for government revenue.

As it happens, the Alberta government this week revised its fiscal 2026-27 projections, as the oil-rich province now forecasts a C$2 billion surplus as opposed to a C$9 billion deficit. The change is the result of sharply higher energy prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East, which has brought oil-tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz to an effective halt.

Canada said that for June, total income-tax revenue fell 5.1%, due to a deep drop in corporate receipts. Total revenue was flat in the month, with the level largely unchanged from the same year-ago month at C$44.82 billion. Total expenses in June rose 6.4%, to C$43.83 billion, due to the rollout of a sales-tax credit to households and a 12%-plus increase in debt-financing costs.

For the April-to-June period, total tax receipts climbed 7.4% from a year ago, while total revenue jumped nearly 10%. Total expenses in the first quarter climbed by a more moderate 4.6% from the same year-ago period.
